title: Tilt a stand mixer's head back: hold its sprung lock lever up, lift the 4.5 kg head to its stop, let the lever lock it
instruction: Tilt the stand mixer's head all the way back and leave it locked in the up position, with your hands off the mixer.
context: Close to half of US consumers own a stand mixer (43%, AHAM 2018). On a tilt-head one, such as KitchenAid's Classic or Artisan, the head is tipped back every time the bowl or beater goes on or comes off. KitchenAid's K45 manual: 'Push locking lever up into UNLOCK position and hold. Tilt motor head back. Move locking lever into LOCK position.' Let the lever go before the head has moved and the head stays locked down; let the head go before it is locked up and it drops forward onto the bowl clamp, since in the model its weight is ahead of the hinge (an estimate) all the way to the stop, about 31 degrees. The head weighs about 4.5 kg (estimate): lifting it by its hub takes about 15 N at the start and 8 N at the stop, along the hinge's arc, while the other hand holds the sprung lever up on the column's side, 31 cm away. Unlike holding a release while sliding a light part, the part freed here is a 4.5 kg head, lifted on an arc and carried to its stop before it may be let go.
setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the arm bases: x forward, y to the robot's left; heights above the bench top. (1) A tilt-head stand mixer at the published size of the KitchenAid Classic K45SS: 35.3 cm high, 22.1 wide, 35.8 deep, and 43.9 cm high with the head up (KitchenAid's figure for its tilt-head mixers). White enamel-painted head and stand, chrome attachment-hub cap, beater shaft and bowl clamping plate, dark grey plastic lever tab, black rubber feet. It stands free on its feet (stand 5 kg, head 4.5 kg, foot friction 0.8, all estimates), base centre at (39.4, -8.9), turned so that its front faces the robot and the left arm: the head points from its hinge toward (24.9, -0.5). (2) The head turns on a hinge pin across the column top at (49.4, -14.7, 19.5), from 0 degrees (down, locked) to its up stop at 30.8 degrees, the angle at which the mixer reaches 43.9 cm. Its centre of mass (estimate: the centroid of the modelled head) is 10.2 cm ahead of the pin and 6.8 cm above it, so in the model its weight pulls it forward at every angle up to the stop. The attachment hub, 5 cm across and 4 cm proud of the head's front, is centred at (24.9, -0.5, 26.3) with the head down. (3) The locking lever: a tab 2.5 cm long and 1.2 cm high standing 1.8 cm out of the column's right side (the mixer's right as you face its front), centred at (44.9, -20.3, 13.4), at LOCK. It slides 1 cm up to UNLOCK against a 5 N return spring (travel and force are estimates) and springs back to LOCK when let go, as KitchenAid's 5K45 manual gives it: 'Once lifted, the lever will automatically go back in LOCK position to keep the head lifted.' The real trial uses a KitchenAid 5K45SS, whose manual gives that up-lock (KitchenAid says the up-lock is on 'select models' only). (4) The lock: the pin holds the hinge while the lever is under 7 mm up and the head is within 1 degree of its down stop or 0.5 degrees of its up stop; with the lever 7 mm or more up the head is free. No bowl or beater is fitted. The arms start at their ready pose, clear of the mixer.
scoring: Judged on the state at the end, held 1 s; only failures latch. Terms. Up: head angle 10 degrees or more (real trial: a digital angle gauge, 0.1 degree, about USD 30, on the head's top). At the stop: within 2 degrees of the up stop. Locked up: at the stop with the lever under 2 mm from LOCK (real trial: a ruler on the tab), the pin in and every fingertip 3 cm or more from the mixer for 1 s (real trial: a 3 cm gauge block between each fingertip and the mixer); then a 10 N push down the head's arc at the hub, applied by the scorer for 0.5 s, must move it under 1 degree (real trial: a 1 kg weight hung on the hub, read on the gauge). Tiers: locked up and the push held, 1.0; at the stop but not locked up (held there by a hand, or the lever held at UNLOCK), 0.5; locked up but moved 1 degree or more by the push, 0.5, whatever the head does after it; up but short of the stop, 0.25; otherwise 0. Zeros that stick: the head meets either stop faster than 120 degrees a second, dropped or flung (real trial: 240 fps phone video), or the mixer slides over 2 cm or tips over 5 degrees (real trial: tape marks round its feet). Free: time on the lever, regrips, which hand does what. Possible scores 0, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0.
run_limit: 1,200 steps (60 s at 20 Hz); the scripted demo reaches 1.0 at step 391 (19.6 s) on RTX 4070 Ti SUPER and 497 (24.9 s) on an RTX 5090.
reset_notes: About 30 s (estimate), nothing consumed: hold the lever at UNLOCK, lower the head gently by the hub until it is fully down, let the lever return to LOCK and check the head will not lift; set the feet back on their tape marks. No hidden variables; no seed changes the scene.
fidelity: The mixer at the K45SS's published outer size, shaped from photos (no CAD). Estimates: head 4.5 kg and its centre of mass, hinge place, stand 5 kg, lever spring 5 N over 10 mm, foot friction 0.8. So an unlocked head's forward fall at the stop is an estimate, not measured on a real mixer (the manual locks it up 'to keep the head lifted'). The up stop comes from the published 43.9 cm head-up height. The lock pin is a rule only the lever's travel, moved by the robot, releases. Demo reads joints.
